struct_fields.comment:
base IC written by the daily IC calculation

**Renamed from `base_ic` 2026-10-05: it is anything but base.** The game's own accessor is `CCountry::GetTotalIC` (rva 0x23670 = `mov eax,[ecx+0x604]; ret`), and this entry's own neighbour at +0x60C already describes why that is the right word. CCountry::UpdateIC writes the summed province base to +0x604 **and** +0x60C from one register at 0xF0F9D/0xF0FA3, and then only +0x604 is touched again: scaled by (1000 + countryValues[GLOBAL_IC] + technologyStatus ic_bonus) / 1000 and floored at 1 (0xF0FA9-0xF0FEB), cut to what metal and energy support (0xF14A6), and finally topped up with the resource-free lend-lease IC (0xF14C1). So +0x60C is the base and +0x604 is the total actually delivered. The event keyword agrees from the other side: `CTotalICTrigger::Evaluate` compares its threshold against **+0x604**, so the script's `total_ic` and the Lua API's `TotalIC` are the same field under the same name.

struct_fields.name: MaxInfrastructure
struct_fields.comment:
An int in thousandths that the unit AI uses as "is this province worth holding a front over". `CAIUnit::EstimateAreaNeed` requires a neighbour's value to be at least 200 before the province counts as a front (0x4B8830), and gives the province itself the floor weight 500 instead of 1000 when its own value is at or below 300 (0x4B8BF4). Eight more readers across the unit AI and the map code. **Written in exactly one place**: `CProvince::LoadKey`'s default arm, which treats an unknown key as a building name and, when the loaded building's definition `+0x24` is 12, sets `province->+0x5C = building->level(+0x20) * definition->+0x8 / 1000` (0x96132-0x96152). Which building type index 12 is was **not** established - the mod reorders `common/buildings.txt`, so it is not safe to count. The cheapest live check is `dumpStruct.py` on a province and a comparison against the province panel.

**Confirmed live 2026-10-02, and renamed from `ai_front_value`.** Read on every province with an `infra` key in `history/provinces/`, and compared: **10,642 of 10,642 agree** with `infra * 100`, where `infra` is the file's 0-10 value. (A first pass scored 98.43% against the *first* `infra` key in each file; all 167 misses were files that repeat the key, and the engine is **last-wins** - the residual was the test, not the field.) This does not contradict 'an int in thousandths': `infra * 100` and a fraction in thousandths are the same number, since the file's 0-10 is 0-100%. Paris (2613) reads 1000 = infra 10.0 = 100%.

**The old name named a use, not the field.** The unit AI reads infrastructure when deciding whether a province is worth holding a front over, which is why it looked like an AI value. The gain from the rename is that the thresholds become readable in the units a modder sees: the 200 at 0x4B8830 is **infrastructure 2.0** and the 300 at 0x4B8BF4 is **3.0**. A province under 2.0 does not count as a front; under 3.0 it gets the floor weight 500 instead of 1000.

`+0x24 == 12` is untouched by this and is still not a building index - `infra` is building no.21 in the mod's `common/buildings.txt`, so 12 is an id of something else, as the record already says.

**Renamed from `infrastructure` and retyped 2026-10-05, in step with CProvince +0x5C**, which is the same field: RTTI has CMapProvince deriving from CProvince at offset 0, and both structures carry it only because Ghidra has no inheritance. The game's own name is `MaxInfrastructure`, from `CProvince::GetMaxInfrastructure` (rva 0x6C360); the effective infrastructure is a different quantity computed by `CProvince::GetInfrastructure` (rva 0x94570) out of the modifier array at +0x114. The unit AI's use of this field - a neighbour needing at least 200 before a province counts as a front, the floor weight dropping to 500 at or below 300 - is unchanged by the rename and now reads as thresholds on 20% and 30% of full infrastructure, which is what the 1000 clamp in GetInfrastructure says the scale is.

struct_fields.comment: The game's own name for it, out of the Lua API. `CAIStrategy::GetPersonality` (rva 0x16000) is `mov eax, dword ptr [ecx + 0x18]; ret` - the whole function, so the function *is* the offset. struct_fields.evidence: The Lua half has had this field all along and project.json has not, which is the whole of what this entry claims. `scripts/reconcileFacts.py --accessors` re-derives it from hoi3_tfh.exe: `luabindExtract.accessor_field` accepts only a two-instruction body - one read of a member and a bare `ret` - or one of three strict by-value shapes, so it either reproduces the registered offset or reports nothing at all. All 207 of the Lua half's accessor-derived fields re-derive, over 173 distinct addresses, this one among them. The name and the class come from the registration, not from the body. What would show it wrong: the body decoding as something other than the text above, or the registration turning out to name a different class - and the risk a shared body does carry is on the function's name, which is why the holder counts are quoted and why nothing here names a function. `mergeFindings --check` is the backstop for the offset already being recorded under another name; it reports none of these as taken.

That body is shared - 3 luabind registrations (CGovernmentPosition::GetIndex, CLaw::GetIndex, CMinisterType::GetIndex) and 0 virtual table slots - so it cannot carry a class name, but the field can: the registration is what names the class, and a linker fold of identical getters says nothing about either class's layout.
struct_fields.evidence: The Lua half has had this field all along and project.json has not, which is the whole of what this entry claims. `scripts/reconcileFacts.py --accessors` re-derives it from hoi3_tfh.exe: `luabindExtract.accessor_field` accepts only a two-instruction body - one read of a member and a bare `ret` - or one of three strict by-value shapes, so it either reproduces the registered offset or reports nothing at all. All 207 of the Lua half's accessor-derived fields re-derive, over 173 distinct addresses, this one among them. The name and the class come from the registration, not from the body. What would show it wrong: the body decoding as something other than the text above, or the registration turning out to name a different class - and the risk a shared body does carry is on the function's name, which is why the holder counts are quoted and why nothing here names a function. `mergeFindings --check` is the backstop for the offset already being recorded under another name; it reports none of these as taken.
